frase_gancho.texto: A king’s tomb, recreated at full scale under a red light.

puente_narrativo.texto: Beneath that sarcophagus, another face appeared, made of lime and not of green stone. Look for a stucco head, with an elongated profile and three flower buds in its hairstyle.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before a tomb, but it is not the real one. It is a full-scale re-creation of Pakal’s burial chamber, in the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque, the place where the [mask](mna_s09_mascara_pakal) you have just seen was found. A red light falls on the carved slab and on the stone sarcophagus. On the slab, the king appears at the moment of death: he descends along the trunk of a sacred tree toward the jaws of the Earth Monster, the entrance to the underworld. It is interpreted as the step before being reborn. On the walls there are stucco figures: they are the Nine Lords of the Night. Pakal was buried in the year 683, and his skeleton was covered in cinnabar, a red pigment.

guion_largo.texto:
[The jade mask](mna_s09_mascara_pakal) did not appear in a display case. It appeared in a place, and this is that place, rebuilt at its real size. What you see before you is a re-creation: the true crypt is still in Palenque, more than twenty meters deep, in the heart of the Temple of the Inscriptions, and today it is no longer permitted to go down to it. Here you have the only way to take a glimpse without traveling to Chiapas.

Think about what the builders did. They raised a pyramid of nine levels and, inside it, left a hidden staircase that descends to the king’s chamber. It is thought that Pakal ordered this tomb prepared while he was still alive, and that his son and successor, Kan Bahlam, finished the pyramid that covers it. The king designed his own journey, and his family sealed it with tons of stone.

Look at the great slab that covers the sarcophagus. It weighs several tons, and its relief is read in three levels. Below, the king falls toward the open jaws of the Earth Monster, the gateway to the underworld. In the center grows a sacred tree, shaped like a cross, which joins the worlds. And above, perched at its crown, is a bird of the sky. Pakal is not lying down: he is descending, and the image is interpreted as the beginning of his rebirth.

This scene is so famous that it has given rise to a curious theory: some people have believed they see in it an astronaut steering his rocket. It is not. What looks like a spacecraft is the king’s body above the jaws of the earth, and what look like tubes are part of the tree and of the monster. There are no astronauts, but a very beautiful Maya idea: a king who dies in order to be reborn, like the maize seed that is buried and sprouts again.

Notice also the sides of the original sarcophagus. There, a row of figures was carved who are thought to be the king’s ancestors, and from each one a tree laden with fruit springs. Pakal did not arrive alone in the other world: his lineage welcomed him.

Now look at the walls, where there are stucco figures. They are nine lords standing, the Nine Lords of the Night, who, it is thought, watched over the king’s sleep. The number nine is no accident: nine were the levels of the pyramid that covers the tomb and, in the Maya tradition, nine were the layers of the underworld. Pakal descended through a pyramid that repeated, in stone, the road that awaited him.

There is one more detail. From the original tomb a stone tube rises alongside the staircase up to the temple. It is thought that it served so that the king’s spirit could communicate with the world of the living. A sealed tomb, but with a thread leading upward.

And there is the color. Pakal’s skeleton was covered in cinnabar, a red pigment that the Maya linked with blood and with the dawn. The red light of this hall reminds you of that color and helps you imagine the chamber closed, for more than one thousand two hundred years, until in 1952 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier opened the door.

Before moving on, one more surprise from that tomb. Beneath the sarcophagus, among ceramic vessels, Ruz found [two stucco heads](mna_s09_cabeza_pakal). You are about to meet one of them now.

texto: Find on the slab the king falling toward the jaws of the Earth Monster
Notice the stucco figures on the walls: they are the Nine Lords of the Night
Watch how the look of the stone changes under the red light

texto.Period: Original from the Late Classic (600-900 AD); museum recreation
texto.Material: Full-scale recreation of a limestone chamber with slab and sarcophagus
texto.Origin: Temple of the Inscriptions, Palenque, Chiapas

texto.pregunta: Myth: The tomb of Pakal that you see here is the original, brought from Palenque.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a full-scale re-creation. The true crypt is still inside the Temple of the Inscriptions, in Palenque.
